content: Nature is the physical, natural, and material world of life that exists without human intervention
Includes landscapes, water and forest ecosystems, weather, organisms, geology, and inanimate objects
Organisms have well-adapted structures that allow them to survive in their immediate environment
Scientists and engineers learn from nature through imitation of physical structures, shapes, materials, and functional mechanisms
Imitation is the process of copying or mimicking biological structures and mechanisms
Scientists sketch biological structures and design functional mechanisms
They tune these into more efficient technologies at macro (large) and nano (very small) scales
The better the understanding of diverse biological materials, the better the ability to develop technologies
Nature serves as a reliable source of knowledge, ideas, and concepts for technology development
Swallow nests have inspired house building design
Weaving technologies developed by studying spider webs
Termite mound architecture inspired building designs with natural climate control
Building designed by imitating termite mound architecture
Termite mounds have chimneys that maintain constant temperature and humidity
The building mimics these natural ventilation and cooling systems
Demonstrates how biomimicry can create energy-efficient structures
Aircraft wings designed by imitating birds and bats
Photograph camera technology imitated from human eyes
Bio-robots designed from kangaroo movement
Injection needle technology copied from mosquito proboscis
Cutting saw imitated from sharp teeth of animals
Synthetic bulletproof vests imitate spider silk
Ceramics imitate crack-resistant shellfish exoskeleton
Robotic arms are imitated from elephant trunk
Sensors in electrical devices imitate biological neurons
These technologies show how nature provides solutions to human problems
Biomimicry is a growing field in engineering and design

Integration of natural and engineering sciences to achieve application of organisms, cells, and molecular analogues for products and services
Examples: using yeasts to produce bread and beer
Benefits include medicinal plants, gene engineering, and biosynthetic materials

sections.section_title: Impacts of Biology and Technology on Society and the Natural World

slides.slide_title: Impacts of Biology on Society and Nature
content: The impact of biology refers to effects arising from advancement of biological knowledge and innovations

Positive impacts include: ensuring food security through increased productivity, improved health and longevity through medicine, better supply of energy and clean water, increased industrial production through microbial action, and antibiotics to treat bacterial infections
Biological weapon production and use destroy the natural world
Predetermining child sex (selecting only XY males) leads to loss of females in society
Technological devices made from biological materials can influence and control society negatively
The misuse of biological information can have harmful effects on both society and the environment

slides.slide_title: Impacts of Technology on Society and Nature
content: Technology is part of everyone's life and has solved many societal problems
Industrialization and technological advancements have resulted in misuse and destruction of the environment
Technologies have damaged our world through: POLLUTION and DEPLETION OF NATURAL RESOURCES
Industrial emissions and effluents pollute clean air and drinking water
Biochemical agents, pesticides, and fertilizers cause toxicity and biohazards
Resource depletion due to overconsumption and inefficient use
These impacts affect human health, biodiversity, and ecosystem function
Ethical issues concern the rightness or wrongness of using biological discoveries for health and wellbeing
Deals with concerns related to biotechnology, medicine, and the environment
Includes questions about the use of biotechnological information, products, or devices on human health
Also includes commercialization of human organs, assisted reproduction techniques, and manipulation of biological systems
Plants are primary producers and feeders for all living organisms
Unethical treatment includes: destructive testing of seeds, cutting tree terminals, overconsumption without conservation, deforestation, burning forests, and restructuring trees for aesthetics
Care for plants is an ethical treatment and important for saving endangered species
It is ethical to plant trees and is a national responsibility
Animals are sentient creatures with nervous systems, capable of feeling pain, stress, and having interests
It is unethical to harm animals during experiments or rigorous testing
Researchers must reduce impacts through the THREE R's PRINCIPLES: Reduction, Refinement, and Replacement
Reduction: Minimize the number of animals used in experiments by improving techniques and sharing information
Refinement: Cleanse experiments to reduce animal suffering using less invasive techniques, better medical care, and better living conditions
Replacement: Substitute animal experiments with alternative techniques using cell cultures, biosynthesis, and computer simulated models

Animals are eukaryotic (cells contain a nucleus)
Animals are multicellular (composed of many cells)
Animals are heterotrophic (obtain food by consuming other organisms)
Animals are sensitive to stimuli and respond to their environment
Animals reproduce, protect themselves, move, respire, excrete, and grow
Animals exhibit different types of body symmetry
Radial symmetry: body parts arranged around a central axis (e.g., starfish)
Bilateral symmetry: left and right sides are mirror images (e.g., humans)
Asymmetry: no symmetry (e.g., sponges)
Animals are categorized into two major groups based on presence or absence of a backbone
VERTEBRATES: Animals with a backbone (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish)
INVERTEBRATES: Animals without a backbone (sponges, worms, insects, crustaceans, mollusks)
Homeothermic (warm-blooded): can maintain constant body temperature (mammals and birds)
Poikilothermic (cold-blooded): body temperature varies with environment (fish, reptiles, amphibians)

Most diverse group of animals in the world

Respiratory system consists of gills or lungs

Involves a single individual and does not require fusion of gametes
More common in invertebrates than vertebrates
Budding: new individual grows from a parent (e.g., hydra)
Fragmentation: parent breaks into pieces, each piece grows into new individual (e.g., starfish)
Parthenogenesis: unfertilized eggs develop into new offspring (e.g., some insects, vertebrates)
Involves two individual parents and requires fusion of gametes from male and female
Produces offspring with genetic material from both parents
Parents are diploid organisms (2n) with complete set of chromosomes
Males produce haploid sperm in testes; females produce haploid eggs (ova) in ovaries
EXTERNAL FERTILIZATION: Eggs are released into the aqueous environment and sperm fertilizes them outside the body (e.g., frogs, fish)
INTERNAL FERTILIZATION: Eggs are fertilized inside the female's body (e.g., mammals, birds, reptiles)
Fertilization of egg by sperm produces a diploid zygote (2n)
Cleavage: series of mitotic cell divisions of the fertilized egg (zygote)
Eight-celled structure is formed, then a hollow structure called blastula
Gastrulation: further cell division and rearrangement, producing a gastrula with different germ layers
Organogenesis: formation of organs during embryonic development from germ layers
Embryo eventually develops into an adult with all tissues, organs, and organ systems

Insects are the largest class of phylum Arthropoda
They have segmented bodies, jointed legs, and exoskeletons
Examples: flies, grasshoppers, lice, butterflies, bees, beetles
Undergo sexual reproduction with internal fertilization in most cases
Some insects undergo parthenogenesis (development from unfertilized eggs)
Series of major changes in body structure as insects develop
Controlled by chemical substances in the insects
Two types of metamorphosis: COMPLETE and INCOMPLETE
Has FOUR stages: Egg → Larva → Pupa → Adult
Example: Honeybee, butterfly, beetle
Larva looks very different from the adult (e.g., caterpillar)
Pupa is a resting, inactive stage where transformation occurs
Adult emerges from the pupa
Has THREE stages: Egg → Nymph → Adult
Example: Grasshopper, cockroach, cricket
Nymph resembles a small adult but lacks wings and reproductive organs
Nymph molts several times, growing larger and developing adult features

Common frog species include: Rana temoraria, Ptychadena goulenger, P. harenna, Leptopelis ragazzi
They do not produce amniotic eggs
Eggs are covered in jelly-like substance to protect them from drying out
Must lay eggs in water to prevent desiccation
External fertilization is most common
Female releases eggs from her body into water
Male releases sperm to fertilize eggs
Internal fertilization occurs in a few species
Lay a large number of eggs in the same place at the same time
Eggs develop into a larval stage called TADPOLE
Tadpole is very different from the adult form
Metamorphosis: tadpole transforms into adult frog
Changes include: developing legs, losing tail, developing lungs
Metamorphosis is controlled by hormones

Reproduce sexually involving both male and female parents
Internal fertilization

Mating takes place under water

Hard, leathery eggs protect the young

The leathery shell prevents desiccation and allows development on land

Reproduce sexually with internal fertilization
Most bird species are monogamous (single male and female for breeding season)
Some are polygamous (multiple partners during breeding season)
Male birds do not have external genital organs
Females have a single ovary
Oviduct consists of several parts with specific functions:
Infundibulum: funnel-shaped upper portion, engulfs the yolk, site of fertilization
Magnum: longest part, secretes albumen (egg white)
Isthmus: forms inner and outer shell membranes
Uterus: forms the shell, egg spends most time here
Vagina: final section, where egg exits through the cloaca
Yolk: contains nutrients for the developing embryo
Chalaza: twisted strands of albumen that anchor the yolk
Albumen (egg white): protein-rich fluid that protects the embryo
Shell membranes: inner and outer membranes
Air sac: provides oxygen for the embryo
Shell: hard, porous outer layer for protection
Incubation: keeping eggs warm while embryos develop
Females usually incubate, but males sometimes participate
Brood patch: area of skin with blood vessels for heat transfer
Birds rotate eggs periodically for even warmth distribution
Hatching: chick uses an egg tooth (hard tip at beak) to break the shell
Egg tooth is lost after hatching
Nest building in hidden areas to avoid predators
Some birds lay eggs on bare cliffs (no nest)
Camouflaged eggs help protect from predators
Parental care varies widely: from no care to extended care
In some species, care ends at hatching; in others, care continues for extended time

The observable actions and responses of animals to stimuli
Includes movements, interactions within and with the environment
Also includes learning about their environment
Behavior can be categorized into two main types: INNATE and LEARNED
Inborn behavior that is determined by genes
Independent of experience
Specific to a species
Three types: INSTINCTIVE, REFLEXIVE, ORIENTATIVE
INSTINCTS: Complex behaviors specific to a species
Examples: web making in spiders, nest-building in birds, swimming in dolphins, chicks opening mouths for food, honeybee dance
REFLEXES: Simple, involuntary responses to stimuli
Examples: pulling hand away from hot object, blinking when something approaches eye, closing eyes when dust enters
TAXIS: Directed movement in response to a stimulus
Positive taxis: movement towards the stimulus
Negative taxis: movement away from the stimulus
Examples: phototaxis (light), chemotaxis (chemicals), thigmotaxis (touch), geotaxis (gravity)
KINESIS: Undirected, random movement in response to a stimulus
Example: movement of woodlice in response to temperature
Not inherited, not determined by genes
Acquired during the lifetime of an individual
Allows adaptation to changes in environment
Modified by previous experiences
Habituation: stopping response to repeated stimulus (e.g., ignoring TV sound)
Classical conditioning: associating a neutral stimulus with a significant one (Pavlov's dogs)
Operant conditioning: learning through rewards and punishments (Skinner's experiments)
Sensitization: increased response to repeated stimulus
Latent learning: learning without immediate reward
Insight learning: using past experience and reasoning to solve problems
Stage 1 - Before conditioning: Unconditioned stimulus produces unconditioned response (food causes salivation)
Stage 2 - During conditioning: Conditioned stimulus (bell) paired with unconditioned stimulus (food)
Stage 3 - After conditioning: Conditioned stimulus alone produces conditioned response (bell causes salivation)
Learning through consequences
Reinforcers: responses that increase the probability of behavior being repeated (positive or negative)
Punishers: responses that decrease the likelihood of behavior being repeated
Behavior likely to be repeated when reinforced, less likely when punished

Common behavioral patterns exhibited by many species
Examples include: behavioral cycles, reproductive behavior, social behavior, competition, territory, communication
Animals respond to periodic changes in the environment
Can be daily or seasonal cycles
Seasonal migration: movement from one habitat to another due to food availability, temperature, breeding conditions
Circadian rhythms: 24-hour cycles (sleep-wake cycle), also called biological clocks
Reproductive behavior: locating and selecting mates, producing offspring, rearing them to independence
Includes courtship displays (visual, sounds, chemicals)
Social behavior: commonly observed in animals that live in groups
Examples: ants, termites, bees (division of labor as workers and soldiers), elephants, penguins, humans
Competition: animals compete for resources (space, territory, water, mates, food)
Intraspecific competition: between individuals of the same species
Interspecific competition: between individuals of different species
Territoriality: defending a space containing resources needed for survival
Display behavior: used instead of fighting, safer and uses less energy
Vital for interaction between animals
Can communicate using: sight (visual displays), sound (birds singing, frogs croaking), touch (tactile), chemicals (pheromones)
Pheromones: special chemicals used for communication
Example: ants use pheromones to mark trails to food sources
Male dogs and lions use urine pheromones to mark territory

Homeostasis is the self-regulatory process by which animals maintain stable internal conditions in their bodies regardless of external conditions
Helps animals maintain equilibrium in the internal conditions of their bodies at a set point (normal conditions)
Body systems constantly adjust to internal and external changes
STIMULUS: A change in the environment that forces the organism to respond
RECEPTOR: Detects the change and sends a signal to the control center
CONTROL CENTER: Receives the signal, interprets it, and sends commands (hypothalamus in the brain)
EFFECTOR: Acts on the stimulus based on the command, counteracting the change
Thermoregulation is the process of maintaining internal body temperature constant
Organisms use behavior, physiology, and morphology to keep body temperatures within optimal level
Two groups based on temperature regulation: POIKILOTHERMIC and HOMEOTHERMIC
Body temperature is the same as or similar to the environment
Lack internal control over body temperature
Use behavioral methods to regulate: burrowing into ground, sunning on rocks, swimming, group activity
Examples: fish, reptiles, amphibians
Can generate internal heat to maintain constant body temperature
Cellular processes operate optimally even when environment is cold or hot
Use morphological, physiological, and behavioral methods
Methods for COLD: insulation (fur, fat, feathers), vasoconstriction, shivering
Methods for HOT: vasodilation, sweating
RADIATION: Heat loss through electromagnetic waves
EVAPORATION: Heat loss through sweating
CONVECTION: Heat transfer through air or water currents
CONDUCTION: Heat transfer through direct contact
Osmoregulation is the process of regulating osmotic pressure of fluids and electrolytic balance
About 60% of the human body is composed of fluids
2/3 of water content is in intracellular fluids, 1/3 is extracellular fluid
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect changes in osmotic pressure
Kidneys are the main organ responsible for osmoregulation
Glucose is the main source of energy for normal body functioning
Two hormones from the pancreas control blood glucose: INSULIN and GLUCAGON
INSULIN: lowers blood glucose level by converting glucose to glycogen in the liver
GLUCAGON: raises blood glucose level by converting glycogen to glucose in the liver
Glycogen is stored in the liver and can be converted back to glucose when needed
NEGATIVE FEEDBACK: Reverses the direction of the stimulus, bringing the body back to the set point (most common)
POSITIVE FEEDBACK: Amplifies the change, pushing the body further away from homeostasis (e.g., childbirth contractions)
Negative feedback has three components: sensor (receptor), control center, effector

Enzymes are protein molecules that act as biological catalysts (biocatalysts)
They accelerate the rate of chemical reactions by lowering activation energy
Activation energy is the minimum amount of energy required for a reaction to occur
All enzymes are made up of chains of amino acids linked by peptide bonds
Enzymes are essential for metabolism (breakdown and synthesis of molecules)
Enzymes act upon molecules called SUBSTRATES
They convert substrates into products of different molecules
Enzymes remain unchanged after the reaction (can be reused)
The active site is where the substrate binds
The enzyme-substrate complex is formed during the reaction
Objective: Investigate the enzyme Salivary Amylase in the mouth
Material: White bread
Procedure: Chew a piece of bread slowly, notice the changing flavor (tastes sweeter)
Control experiment: Mix bread in water for 5 minutes and compare taste
Assessment: How does saliva convert starch into maltose? Where did the enzyme amylase come from?
DENATURATION: Breaking of non-covalent bonds, distorting shape and active site; caused by high heat, extreme pH, heavy metals, high salt concentrations
SOLUBILITY: Dissolve in water, salt solutions, dilute glycerol
COLLOIDAL NATURE: Large size prevents dialysis across semipermeable membrane
BIOCATALYST: Very small quantity converts large quantity of substrate
PRECIPITATION: Separated for analysis using aqueous or ethanol solvents
HIGH MOLECULAR WEIGHT: Large protein biomolecules
HEAT AND PH SENSITIVITY: Activated at optimum temperature and pH
REGULATION: Controlled by activator and inhibitor molecules
CATALYSIS: High catalytic efficiency; can transform 100-10,000 substrates per second
REVERSIBILITY: Can catalyze reactions in both forward and reverse directions
SPECIFICITY: Restrictive in choice of substrate (bond, group, substrate, optical, co-factor specificity)
Speed up chemical reactions in the human body
Essential for respiration, digestion, liver, muscle, and nerve function
Each cell contains thousands of enzymes
Turnover number: substrates converted by one enzyme molecule per second at saturated active sites
Enzymes are markers of diseases like myocardial infarction, jaundice, pancreatitis, cancer

slides.slide_title: Examples of Enzymes and Their Functions
content: Sucrase: breaks down sucrose into glucose and fructose
Lactase: breaks down lactose into glucose and galactose
Carbohydrase: breaks down carbohydrates into sugars
Lipase: breaks down fats into fatty acids
Protease: breaks down proteins into amino acids
Step 1: Substrate (sucrose) consists of glucose and fructose bonded together
Step 2: Substrate binds to enzyme, forming enzyme-substrate complex
Step 3: Binding places stress on the bond and the bond breaks
Step 4: Products are released, enzyme is free to bind other substrates
Enzymes perform their function by lowering a reaction's activation energy
Lipases: Split fats found in blood, gastric juices, pancreatic secretions, intestinal juices, adipose tissues
Amylase: Exists in saliva, changes starches into sugars
Maltase: Exists in foods like potatoes, pasta, beer; breaks maltose into glucose
Trypsin: Found in small intestine, breaks proteins into amino acids
Lactase: Found in small intestine, breaks lactose into glucose and galactose
Helicase: Unwinds DNA
DNA Polymerase: Forms new copies of DNA
Acetylcholinesterase: Breaks down neurotransmitter acetylcholine in nerves and muscles

Enzymes are proteins
Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds
Proteins have four structural levels: PRIMARY, SECONDARY, TERTIARY, QUATERNARY
Humans require 20 amino acids: 10 synthesized in the body, 10 obtained from diet
Linear sequence of amino acids
Amino acids linked together to form a polypeptide chain through peptide bonds
Proteins with fewer than 50 sequences are peptides
Proteins with longer than 50 sequences are polypeptides
Sequence determines the protein's final structure and function
Folded structure formed within a polypeptide due to interactions between atoms of the backbone
Stabilized by hydrogen bonding
Two main types: ALPHA-HELIX and BETA-PLEATED SHEET
ALPHA-HELIX: Right-handed coiled strand; side-chain substituents extend to the outside; hydrogen bonds between CO and NH groups stabilize the structure

sections.section_title: The Structure and Function of DNA and RNA

content: DNA has a ladder-like double helix structure twisted into a spiral shape
Sugar and phosphate groups form the two vertical sides of the ladder
Nitrogenous bases form the rungs
Consists of two long chains called polynucleotides
Nucleotides are the basic building blocks of DNA
Each nucleotide is composed of:
SUGAR: Deoxyribose
PHOSPHATE GROUP
NITROGENOUS BASE: One of four types
Four types of nitrogenous bases:
Adenine (A)
Thymine (T)
Guanine (G)
Cytosine (C)
A and G are PURINES (double-ring structures)
C and T are PYRIMIDINES (single-ring structures)
Base pairing: A pairs with T, C pairs with G
Sugar (deoxyribose) and phosphate form the backbone
Nitrogenous bases form hydrogen bonds between the two strands
Each strand has polarity: 5' end and 3' end
The two strands run in opposite directions (antiparallel)
James Watson and Francis Crick discovered the double helix structure
GENES: Sections of DNA that contain instructions for characteristics; basic structural and functional units of inheritance
CHROMOSOMES: Threadlike structures made of protein (histone) and DNA molecules
Each chromosome may contain hundreds to thousands of genes
Locus (Loci): The specific position of a gene on a chromosome
Chromosomes exist in pairs in diploid organisms (one from each parent)
Human cells contain 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs
22 pairs are autosomes (non-sex chromosomes)
1 pair are sex chromosomes (XX for females, XY for males)
Karyotype: A picture of an individual's chromosomes arranged in pairs
Store all genetic information needed to grow, develop, reproduce, control the cell, and survive
Determines the characteristics of an organism
Carries and transmits hereditary material from parents to offspring
Transmission occurs through DNA replication during cell division
DNA replication is the process by which DNA makes a copy of itself during cell division
Essential for transfer of genetic information from one cell to its daughters and from one generation to the next
DNA gives rise to RNAs through transcription
DNA replication is SEMICONSERVATIVE
Each strand in the DNA double helix acts as a template for the synthesis of a new, complementary strand
The two original DNA strands separate during replication
Each strand serves as a template for a new DNA strand
Each newly synthesized double helix is a combination of one old and one new DNA strand
DNA HELICASE: Binds to double-stranded DNA and stimulates separation of the two strands
DNA POLYMERASE: Adds new nucleotides to a growing strand and links DNA bases in the correct sequence
RNA PRIMASE: Synthesizes RNA primers complementary to the DNA strand
DNA LIGASE: Links two fragments of DNA by forming a phosphodiester bond
TOPOISOMERASE: Prevents supercoiling at the region ahead of the replication fork
STAGE 1: DNA helix is unwound and unzipped; hydrogen bonds between bases break; double helix separates into two strands
STAGE 2: The two separated strands act as templates; DNA polymerase adds free nucleotides using complementary base pairing (A-T and C-G)
STAGE 3: The two new strands twist to form a double helix; each is identical to the original strand
Replication fork: The Y-shaped structure formed during DNA replication due to unwinding and separation of the two strands
LEADING STRAND: Synthesized continuously in the same direction as the growing replication fork
LAGGING STRAND: Synthesized discontinuously in the opposite direction of the growing replication fork

Enables growth, repair of damaged tissues, and reproduction of organisms
Information stored in DNA transfers from one cell to another through cell division
DNA replicates during cell division
The cell cycle is an ordered series of events involving cell growth and division
Two major phases:
INTERPHASE: Preparation for cell division (growth, nutrient gathering, DNA replication)
MITOTIC PHASE (M PHASE): Cell division itself
G1 PHASE (First Gap): Cell accumulates building blocks of DNA and proteins; builds energy reserves
S PHASE (Synthesis): DNA replication proceeds; sister chromatids are formed

Mitosis is the division of somatic cells (body cells)
Produces two genetically identical daughter cells
Occurs in growth, repair, and replacement of cells
Multistep process: Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase (PMAT)
PROPHASE: Nuclear envelope dissociates; chromosomes condense and become visible; centrosomes move to opposite poles
METAPHASE: Chromosomes align at the metaphase plate (equator); sister chromatids attached to microtubules
ANAPHASE: Sister chromatids separate and are pulled to opposite poles
TELOPHASE: Chromosomes reach poles and decondense; nuclear envelopes reform
CYTOKINESIS: Cytoplasmic division; two genetically identical daughter cells
Meiosis is the division that produces sex cells (gametes)
Has two phases: Meiosis I and Meiosis II
Produces four genetically different daughter cells with haploid number of chromosomes
Reduces chromosome number by half
Increases genetic variation through crossing over and independent assortment
PROPHASE I: Chromosomes condense; homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis); crossing over occurs; nuclear envelope disintegrates
METAPHASE I: Homologous pairs align at the equator; spindle fibers attach to one chromosome of each pair
ANAPHASE I: Homologous chromosomes separate and are pulled to opposite poles
TELOPHASE I: Chromosomes complete move; nuclear envelopes reform; cytokinesis produces two daughter cells
Crossing over occurs during Prophase I of meiosis
Non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange segments of DNA
Results in new combinations of alleles (genetic variation)
Increases variability within a population
PROPHASE II: Chromosomes condense again in each daughter cell; nuclear membrane dissolves; spindle forms
METAPHASE II: Sister chromatids line up end-to-end at the equator
ANAPHASE II: Sister chromatids separate and are pulled to opposite poles
TELOPHASE II: Chromosomes complete move; nuclear membranes reform; cytokinesis produces four haploid cells
MITOSIS: One division; two daughter cells; diploid; genetically identical; somatic cells
MEIOSIS: Two divisions; four daughter cells; haploid; genetically different; gametes
Mitosis: no crossing over; Meiosis: crossing over occurs
Mitosis: growth and repair; Meiosis: reproduction

Gregor Mendel, an Austrian monk, is considered the father of genetics
He studied how traits are passed from one generation to the next using garden peas (Pisum sativum)
He discovered two foundational principles of inheritance:
LAW OF SEGREGATION
LAW OF INDEPENDENT ASSORTMENT
Gene: A segment of DNA that determines a trait
Allele: Alternative form of a gene (e.g., T for tall, t for short)
Dominant: The expressed trait in a heterozygote (represented by a capital letter)
Recessive: The masked trait in a heterozygote (represented by a lowercase letter)
Genotype: The genetic makeup of an organism (e.g., TT, Tt, tt)
Phenotype: The observable physical characteristics (e.g., tall, short)
Homozygous: Two identical alleles (e.g., TT or tt)
Heterozygous: Two different alleles (e.g., Tt)
Mendel studied seven pairs of contrasting traits:
Seed form: Round (dominant) vs. Wrinkled (recessive)
Seed color: Yellow (dominant) vs. Green (recessive)
Pod form: Inflated (dominant) vs. Constricted (recessive)
Pod color: Green (dominant) vs. Yellow (recessive)
Flower color: Purple (dominant) vs. White (recessive)
Flower position: Axial (dominant) vs. Terminal (recessive)
Stem length: Tall (dominant) vs. Short (recessive)
A cross between two parents to study the inheritance of a SINGLE trait
Mendel crossed true-breeding (pure) parents with contrasting traits
Example: Tall (TT) x Short (tt)
F1 GENERATION: All heterozygous (Tt), all tall (dominant trait expressed)
F1 self-cross (Tt x Tt) produces F2 GENERATION
F2 generation from Tt x Tt:
GENOTYPIC RATIO: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt
PHENOTYPIC RATIO: 3 Tall : 1 Short
This demonstrates the LAW OF SEGREGATION
The 3:1 ratio was observed for all seven traits Mendel studied
Mendel's first law of heredity
States that copies of genes randomly separate or segregate during meiosis
Each gamete receives only one allele
The physical basis is the first division of meiosis
Homologous chromosomes with their different versions of each gene are segregated into daughter nuclei

States that genes do not influence each other with regard to the sorting of alleles into gametes

Process in the seminiferous tubules of the testis
Primordial germ cells (PGCs) divide by mitosis to produce spermatogonia (diploid)
Spermatogonia undergo mitosis to form primary spermatocytes
Primary spermatocytes undergo meiosis I → two secondary spermatocytes (haploid)

Process in the ovaries
Oogonia (diploid) undergo mitosis and then meiosis to form primary oocytes

Population ecology is the study of how populations interact with their environment
Examines distribution, abundance, and changes in populations over time
A POPULATION is a group of individuals of the same species living and interbreeding in a given area
Ecological organization: Individual → Population → Community → Ecosystem → Biome → Biosphere
POPULATION SIZE (N): Total number of individuals present in a particular habitat
POPULATION DENSITY: Number of individuals per unit area or volume
Formula: Density = N / Area
Counting all individuals is often difficult; SAMPLING methods are used
Important for understanding resource needs and environmental impact
CLUMPED DISPERSION: Individuals clustered in groups (most common)
RANDOM DISPERSION: Individuals distributed randomly, no predictable pattern (rare)
UNIFORM DISPERSION: Individuals spaced more or less evenly
Dispersion provides information about interactions and resource distribution
QUADRAT METHOD: Used for plants and immobile organisms
A square frame is placed randomly; organisms within are counted
Formula: Estimated population = (Total area / Sample area) × Number counted
MARK-RECAPTURE METHOD: Used for mobile animals
Formula: N = (M × n) / X
M = number marked in first capture; n = number recaptured; X = number marked in recapture
CENSUS: Systematic collection of information from all individuals in a population
DE FACTO METHOD: Census conducted on a fixed date (e.g., full-moon night)
DE JURE METHOD: Census conducted over 2-3 weeks; only permanent residents counted

Describes population growth in an environment with unlimited resources
Population increases at a constant rate (r)
r = B - D (Birth rate - Death rate)
r > 0: Population increasing; r = 0: No change; r < 0: Population decreasing
Growth rate: dN/dt = rN
Results in a J-SHAPED CURVE
Describes population growth with limited resources
CARRYING CAPACITY (K): Maximum population size the environment can sustain
Growth rate slows as population approaches K
Equation: dN/dt = rN (K-N)/K
Results in an S-SHAPED (SIGMOID) CURVE
EXPONENTIAL: Unlimited resources; J-shaped curve; no carrying capacity
LOGISTIC: Limited resources; S-shaped curve; has carrying capacity (K)
Real populations show logistic growth due to resource limitations
Exponential growth is theoretical and not sustainable
